title: Cultural Jews
hookLine: some Jews connect through culture, food, humor and history more than belief

lines: THE SAME JOKE AS LAST YEAR.
cards: A Friday night kitchen. Someone is braiding challah from a grandmother's recipe, flour up to the elbows. An uncle tells the same joke he told last year, and everyone groans on cue.
A cousin who hasn't set foot in a synagogue in years is arguing hard about a piece of Jewish history. Ask any of them whether they believe in God, and you may get a shrug, a long story, or a laugh.
Ask whether they're Jewish, and the answer comes fast: of course.

teach.h: WHAT MEAN YE BY THIS SERVICE?
teach.b: The Torah expects a question. About the Passover meal, Exodus says: "when your children shall say unto you: What mean ye by this service?" Not if.
When. The tradition plans for the one who isn't sure what any of this is for.

teach.h: FOUR CHILDREN, ALL AT THE TABLE.
teach.b: The Haggadah, the book read at the seder, turns that into four children. One is wise. One is called wicked, because he says this service is for you, not for him.
One is simple. And one doesn't even know how to ask. All of them are at the table.

The Haggadah has an answer for each, and for the child who can't ask, it tells the parent to open the conversation. Even the one called wicked gets an answer, a blunt one, and he is still counted among the four.

Then a line from the Talmud that later rabbis leaned on: an Israelite, even one who has sinned, is still an Israelite. Some teachers read it as a statement about belonging that doubt doesn't switch off.

teach.h: A PEOPLE, NOT ONLY A CREED.
teach.b: That's why the Hebrew word am, a people, matters here. For some Jews, the way in isn't a creed.
It's Yiddish words in a grandparent's mouth, a pot of soup, a shelf of books, a sense of humor, a history carried in the body. Communities respond in different ways.
Humanistic Jewish congregations build their whole life around culture, history and ethics.
Some Orthodox outreach teachers see the kitchen and the joke as a doorway, and gently invite people further in, toward Shabbat and the commandments. Others stand in between.
Culture counts: it's one of the real ways people stay at the table.

how: Some Jews express their Jewishness mostly through food, holidays at home, humor, language, books, music and history, and Jewish communities range from Humanistic congregations built on culture and ethics to Orthodox outreach that invites people toward more observance.

o: people of other faiths who enjoy Jewish holidays
Jews who keep every commandment but never pray
Jews who belong through food, humor, language and history

games.q: you're leading a seder. one child at the table doesn't even know how to ask a question. what does the Haggadah tell you to do?
o: let the child sit quietly and say nothing.
open the conversation for the child yourself.
send the child to play until the meal.
games.why: the Haggadah tells the parent to open the conversation. all four children stay at the table, and each gets an answer.

practice: Find one thing that carries a culture, yours or one you love: a dish, a word only your family uses, a song somebody hummed while cooking. Hold it like an heirloom, and ask who taught it to whom.
If you pray, you can give thanks for the people who carried it to you; if not, just say the name of the person who gave it to you.

wordCard.voice: Cultural Jews. Jews who belong through food, humor, language, books and history, sometimes more than through belief. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a people. Am Yisrael is the people of Israel.

carryVoice: Your line: culture counts. Even a groan at an old joke is a kind of belonging. Same time tomorrow.
